title: Matrix: Rotate Image
oneLiner: Rotate a square matrix 90 degrees clockwise in place: transpose it, then reverse each row.
keyTakeaway: A 90 degree clockwise rotation sends cell (r, c) to (c, n - 1 - r). Doing that directly needs four-way swaps around each ring; the easier route is two simple in-place steps: transpose (swap (r, c) with (c, r) above the diagonal), then reverse every row. Both are O(n²) with O(1) extra space.
explanation:
matrix is n by n. Rotate it 90 degrees clockwise in place (no second matrix) and return it. [[1, 2, 3], [4, 5, 6], [7, 8, 9]] becomes [[7, 4, 1], [8, 5, 2], [9, 6, 3]]: the first column, read bottom to top, becomes the first row.

Look at where a cell goes: the value at row r, column c ends up at row c, column n - 1 - r. Allocating a new matrix and copying every value there is easy but uses O(n²) space. To stay in place, split the move into two steps you can each do with swaps.

Step 1, transpose: swap matrix[r][c] with matrix[c][r] for every c > r, which reflects the matrix across its main diagonal, so (r, c) goes to (c, r). Only loop over the cells above the diagonal; swapping every pair twice puts everything back. Step 2, reverse each row: (c, r) goes to (c, n - 1 - r). Together that is exactly the rotation.

Other rotations are the same trick with a different second step: counter-clockwise is transpose then reverse each column (or reverse each row, then transpose). The direct method, rotating four cells at a time ring by ring, saves the second pass but is easy to get wrong; know the transpose version cold and mention the other.

Every cell is touched a constant number of times: O(n²), which is linear in the size of the matrix, and O(1) extra space. The visualization rotates a 3 by 3 matrix.

visualizationSteps.message: Rotate [[1, 2, 3], [4, 5, 6], [7, 8, 9]] clockwise in place. Step 1 is a transpose.
Swap (0, 1) with (1, 0) across the diagonal: now 4 and 2.
Swap (0, 2) with (2, 0) across the diagonal: now 7 and 3.
Swap (1, 2) with (2, 1) across the diagonal: now 8 and 6.
Transposed: rows became columns. Step 2 reverses each row.
Rotated 90 degrees clockwise: the old first column, read upwards, is the new first row.

recognitionSignals: Rotate or flip a square grid in place: images, game boards, matrices.
A move that maps (r, c) to some mix of r, c and n - 1 - r: break it into a transpose and a reversal.
gotchas: Transposing over the whole matrix instead of only c > r swaps each pair twice and leaves it unchanged.
Reversing columns instead of rows rotates counter-clockwise.
The in-place transpose only works on a square matrix; a rectangular one changes shape and needs a new array.
confusableWith: Spiral Order also works ring by ring, but only reads values; nothing moves.
Reverse an Array In Place is step 2 here, applied to each row.

complexity.note: The matrix is n by n, so it has n² cells; the transpose swaps about n²/2 pairs and the reversals move each cell once more. Everything happens in place.
